opus-5.5.text:
Visualization was really central, almost the whole point. With a standard MLP, the weights are huge matrices of numbers, and even if you plot them you mostly see noise. You can't look at a neuron and say what it's computing.

With KANs, the learnable pieces are one-dimensional functions sitting on the edges. A one-dimensional function is something humans are very good at reading. You plot it and immediately see whether it looks like a sine, a square, an exponential, or roughly linear. So the network stops being an opaque block and becomes a diagram you can actually look at.

That changed how I understood what the network was doing. When I trained on a toy formula, I could watch the structure emerge. Some edges faded away, which told me those inputs didn't matter. Others took on a clear shape, and I could say, "That one is basically a sine." Then you can snap it to the symbolic form, prune what's unnecessary, and sometimes recover the original formula. The visualization wasn't decoration; it was the interface between the human and the model.

It also gave me honesty about failure. Sometimes the plots were messy, and that told me the model hadn't found a clean solution, or that my architecture was wrong for the problem. With a black box, you only see a loss curve going down and have to trust it. Here I could see why the loss was what it was.

More philosophically, it pushed me toward a view I care about a lot: the network as a collaborator for scientists, not just a predictor. If a physicist can look at the learned functions and say, "That looks like a known law," or "That's strange, let's investigate," then the model is participating in discovery. That kind of back-and-forth only works if you can see inside, and visualization made that possible.

r001.rationale: The response explains that plotting KAN edge functions made the network’s internal behavior visible, including what inputs mattered and what functions it learned.

fable-5.1.text:
For me, the whole thing started as a kind of frustration with how opaque neural networks are. When you train a multilayer perceptron, you get a matrix of numbers, and you can stare at those weights all day and learn almost nothing. There's no natural way to "see" what the network has learned.

With KAN, the structure is different. Instead of fixed activation functions on nodes and learnable weights on edges, you put learnable functions on the edges themselves. And those functions are one-dimensional, which means every single one of them can be plotted as a curve. So suddenly the network is not a cloud of numbers, it's a diagram of little graphs. You can look at an edge and say, oh, this one is roughly a sine, that one is quadratic, that one is basically zero and can be pruned.

That changed how I thought about it in a few ways. First, it made debugging intuitive. When something didn't fit, I could literally look at the curves and find where the model was struggling, rather than guessing from a loss curve. Second, it exposed sparsity very directly. A lot of edges go flat after training, and once you see that, pruning becomes obvious rather than a heuristic you bolt on afterward. And third, and this is the part I care most about, it turns the network into something you can have a conversation with. If I'm working with a physicist or a mathematician, I can show them the plot and they can say, that looks like an exponential, or that symmetry looks wrong. They can inject their intuition back into the model. That's a very different relationship than treating it as a black box that you only evaluate on a test set.

So visualization wasn't just a nice-to-have for me. It was the point. The whole motivation was interpretability, and if you can't look at the thing, you don't really know whether you've achieved that.

r001.rationale: The response says that plotting KAN’s learnable edge functions made the network’s learned behavior visible, allowing inspection of curves, sparsity, and model struggles.

astra-6.text: For me, visualizing the CAN network was a way to check whether I actually understood it. You can follow the equations step by step and still miss how the pieces fit together. Drawing it out made those relationships more concrete: what connects to what, how information moves, and where my intuition breaks down. That gave me a clearer sense of what I understood and what I still needed to figure out.

r001.rationale: The response says drawing the network clarified what connects to what and how information moves, communicating that visualization revealed what the network was doing internally.

sol-6.1.text: Visualizing it helped me connect the local computations to the behavior of the whole network. When you only look at equations, it’s easy to lose that connection. Seeing the patterns made it easier to build intuition about how the network worked and then ask more precise questions.

r001.rationale: The response says visualizing the network revealed patterns and helped build intuition about how it worked, communicating that it made the network’s internal behavior visible.
